'''''Robinia neomexicana''''', the '''New Mexican, New Mexico, Southwest, desert, pink,''' or '''rose locust''', is a [[shrub]] or small [[tree]] in the subfamily [[Faboideae]] of the family [[Fabaceae]].

==Distribution==
''Robinia neomexicana'' is native to the [[Southwestern United States]] (southeastern [[California]] and southwestern [[Utah]], [[Virgin River]] region,<ref name=atlas>{{cite book|first=Elbert L.|last=Little Jr.|title=Atlas of United States Trees|volume=3 (Minor Western Hardwoods)|year=1976|publisher=US Government Printing Office|lccn=79-653298|oclc=4053799|entry=Map 162, ''Robinia neomexicana''|entry-url=https://archive.org/details/atlasofunitedsta1314litt/page/n247/mode/1up}}</ref> east through [[Arizona]] and [[New Mexico]], the [[Rio Grande]] valley, to far west [[Texas]]) and adjoining northern [[Mexico]]; from central New Mexico the range extends north into [[Colorado]], mostly the eastern foothills of the [[Rocky Mountains]]. In Arizona, it ranges across the [[Arizona transition zone]], the [[Mogollon Rim]] and [[White Mountains (Arizona)|White Mountains]], and into western and southwestern New Mexico.<ref name=atlas/>

In [[California]], it is uncommon below {{convert|1500|m|ft|abbr=on}} in canyons in the [[Mojave Desert]] and its [[sky island]] [[Single-leaf Pinyon|pinyon]]-[[Juniperus californica|juniper]] [[habitat]]s (''[[Single-leaf Pinyon|Pinus monophylla]]'' and ''[[Juniperus californica]]'').<ref name=Jepson>{{cite web | title = Jepson Manual Treatment | year = 1993 | publisher = University of California | url = https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/cgi-bin/get_JM_treatment.pl?3691,4198,4199 | access-date = 2008-06-18}}</ref> Farther east, it is typically found between {{convert|1200|and|2600|m|ft|abbr=off|sp=us}} along streams, in the bottoms of valleys, and on the sides of canyons.<ref name=Elmore>{{cite book | author=Elmore, Francis H. | title=Trees and Shrubs of the Southwest Uplands | publisher=Western National Parks Association | year=1976 | isbn = 0-911408-41-X | page = 134}}</ref>

==Description==
''Robinia neomexicana'' grows to 5–10 m tall (rarely to 15 m) with bristly shoots. The [[leaf|leaves]] are 10–15 cm long, pinnate with 7–15 leaflets; they have a pair of sharp, reddish-brown thorns at the base. The [[flower]]s are showy and white or pink, and considered fragrant.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.fireflyforest.com/flowers/category/fragrant-flowers-and-plants/|title = Fragrant Flowers and Plants – Southeastern Arizona Wildflowers and Plants}}</ref>  Blooms are produced in spring or early summer in dense [[raceme]]s 5–10 cm long that hang from the branches near the ends.<ref name=Jepson/><ref name=Elmore/>  The fruits are brown bean-like pods with bristles like those on the shoots.<ref name=Elmore/>

==Uses==
In New Mexico, [[Pueblo]] [[Native Americans in the United States|Native Americans]] traditionally ate the flowers uncooked.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Wild plants of the Pueblo Province: exploring ancient and enduring uses|last1=Dunmire|first1=William W.|last2=Tierney|first2=Gail D.|date=1995|publisher=Museum of New Mexico Press|isbn=0-89013-282-8|oclc=32501881}}</ref> The pods were also eaten raw and cooked by some Native Americans, such as the [[Mescalero]] and [[Chiricahua]] Apache.<ref>{{cite book |last=Peattie |first=Donald Culross |author-link=Donald C. Peattie |title=A Natural History of Western Trees |year=1953 |publisher=[[Bonanza Books]] |location=New York |page=592}}</ref>

[[Mule deer]], cattle, and [[goat]]s browse the plant foliage. Cattle also eat the plant's flowers.<ref>{{cite book |last=Little |first=Elbert L. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Western Region |year=1994 |orig-date=1980 |publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50761-4 |edition=Chanticleer Press|page=504}}</ref> [[Squirrel]]s and [[quail]] eat the locust's seeds.<ref name=Elmore/>
